Systemd 221 Fixes Bugs, Wants Distributions To Start Shipping KDBUS

systemd 221 now makes sd-bus.h and sd-event.h public and makes KDBUS support no longer optional. KDBUS support is now always built-in rather than offering a compile-time option. KDBUS support can be disabled at runtime if passing the kdbus=0 option to the kernel command-line.

I'm torn. I like systemd. I like it a lot. It has made my life as a system administrator a lot easier.

But this kind of aggressive attitude makes me see why they get so much hate. I understand it's hard to push against inertia, but I think they would benefit from a little more patiences and at least wait until kdbus is in the mainline.

That's basically how I feel. Overall I like systemd, it's a decent piece of software. I don't have issue with it.

What I do have issue with is that the choice to use other init systems is disappearing. That worries me a little because I don't like lock-in: It makes it hard to rebuild or try a new different design. In that respect what systemd is doing feels like a step back to me.

At least Slackware and Gentoo are SystemD-free bastions.

For now.
And void linux. I realy like the default, runit. It's just so simple and fast. (But nowadays you can't compare systemd with simple init systems)

Gentoo is especially nice in that it makes it trivial to apply patches before installing something, which is great for removing things like the assertion in systemd-init that is used to require it to be run as PID1.
I don't want to start an argument, but you know every distribution can do that, right? Patch the source and compile? They all can.

Yes, any distribution can (and often do) apply patches before generating their packages. What I was referring to is the ability in Gentoo for the user to trivially patch packages, and that's something that's only possibly in a source-based distribution. What's more, the PID1 requirement is a "feature", so convincing a package maintainer to remove it would be difficult; there are no such issues when you can just do it yourself.

The reason systemd got adopted so quickly was because it made life easier for the distribution maintainers (over the users), so features which make it easy for the users to override the decisions of the distribution maintainers are quite relevant.

Why do my server distros NEED to have systemd? I really don't give a toss how fast they boot. I want them to be easy to maintain and easy to do dev-ops shit on them. I hope this doesn't go over well. I really don't like systemd, for the simple reason that it's too large and is not the best tool for the job in some circumstances.
